text:
Some happy news: I’ve been promoted to Senior Software Engineer!

I joined this fintech startup three years ago, and it’s been quite an education. I’ve learned how to build for a business where reliability matters, how to make decisions with incomplete information, and how much better the work gets when you ask for help early.

The best part has been the people. Thanks to the teammates who reviewed my code, challenged my assumptions, and trusted me with bigger problems before I felt entirely ready.

Proud of this milestone, and excited to keep building with this team.

I’m leaving Deloitte to start my own consulting firm.

Writing that sentence feels both exciting and slightly terrifying.

I’ve had the chance to work with some incredibly thoughtful people at Deloitte, and I’m taking a lot of what I learned with me. To the colleagues and clients who made the work worthwhile: thank you.

I’ve wanted to build something of my own for a while. There’s always been a sensible reason to wait another year. This time, I’m giving it a go.

More details soon. For now, I’m looking forward to a new chapter, a steep learning curve, and probably doing my own IT support.

I got laid off last month.

The first few days were mostly logistics: paperwork, updating my CV, working out what the next few months could look like. The feelings caught up later.

I’m still processing it, so I don’t have a neat story about why it was secretly the best thing that ever happened to me.

But I have learned a few things. A job can end even when you care about it and do good work. Asking for help feels awkward until someone says, “Of course.” And a quick message from a former colleague can make a difficult day much easier.

Thank you to everyone who has checked in, made an introduction, or just listened.

Taking it one conversation at a time.

A lot of companies say remote work isn’t working when what they mean is they don’t know how to manage without seeing people at their desks.

So they add more meetings. More status updates. More little green dots to keep an eye on.

Then everyone spends the day proving they’re working and does their actual work in the evening.

Remote work takes some deliberate choices: clear expectations, decisions people can find later, managers who give useful feedback, and room to get things done without being interrupted every 20 minutes.

An office can be great. So can working from home. But moving the same confused process between the two won’t fix it.

We’re hiring two backend engineers in Berlin!

Our stack includes Go and Postgres, and we’re looking for people who enjoy building reliable systems, working through tricky problems, and making technical decisions with their teammates.

If that sounds like your kind of work, send me a message. Happy to share more about the team, the roles, and the interview process.

Know someone who might be interested? Please pass this along or introduce us.

My first manager had a habit I didn’t appreciate enough at the time: when something went wrong, she asked questions before giving an opinion.

What happened? What did we know when we made the decision? What do we need to do now?

There was still accountability. You had to explain your thinking and help fix the problem. But you didn’t have to spend the first half of the conversation defending yourself.

It meant people told her about problems early, while there was still time to do something about them.

I think about that whenever someone brings me bad news. My reaction will probably determine how quickly they bring me the next piece.

We’ve raised a $4M seed round led by Accel!

This gives us the resources to keep building, learn faster from our customers, and grow the team thoughtfully.

Thank you to Accel for believing in what we’re building, and to everyone who has supported us along the way. To our early customers: your feedback has shaped the product more than you know.

And to our team: thank you for the care, persistence, and work that got us here. I’m proud to be doing this with you.

Today we’re taking a moment to celebrate. There’s a lot ahead, and we’re excited to get to it.

AI is making it much easier to produce marketing. It’s also making it much easier to produce marketing nobody wants to read.

A team can now generate a month of posts in an afternoon. That sounds useful until you ask whether any of them say something a customer actually cares about.

The advantage is shifting toward the work around the tools: talking to customers, choosing a clear position, finding a useful insight, and knowing when a draft sounds convincing but says very little.

I’m more interested in using AI to test a few different approaches than to fill every available channel.

If production gets cheaper, judgment deserves more of the budget.

Our new mobile app is live! 🎉

So proud of this team and all the care that went into getting it out the door—from the big product decisions to the tiny details most people will never notice.

Thank you to everyone who built, tested, questioned, and helped us get here. Excited to see people use it, and to learn what we should improve next.

For today, though: we shipped!

Five things I wish I’d heard earlier as a junior developer:

1. Ask questions before you’ve spent an entire day stuck. Share what you tried and where your understanding breaks down.

2. Read the code around your change. The reason something looks strange may be three files away.

3. Make smaller pull requests. They’re easier to review, easier to explain, and much less painful to debug.

4. Get comfortable saying, “I don’t know yet.” Then go find out. Guessing confidently creates extra work for everyone.

5. Learn to describe the problem in plain language. It helps you write better code and makes you a much easier person to work with.

You don’t need to know everything. You do need habits that help you keep learning.

After two years, my first startup has come to an end.

We couldn’t make the business work. That’s hard to write, especially after spending so long telling people why it would.

I made mistakes. I held on to some assumptions too long and was slower than I should have been to admit when things weren’t working. There are decisions I’d make differently now.

I’m proud of the effort we put in, but I’m also disappointed. Both are true.

Thank you to the people who joined us, bought from us, advised us, and supported us outside work. Your time and trust mattered.

I don’t know exactly what comes next. For now, I’m giving myself a little space to finish this chapter properly.

It’s hard to take a company’s mental health messaging seriously when everyone is afraid to take a day off.

Support has to show up in ordinary working life: a realistic workload, a manager who notices when someone is struggling, time off people can actually use, and access to help without having to explain everything to the whole team.

Sometimes a person needs professional support. Sometimes a deadline needs to move. Sometimes both.

We can talk more openly about mental health and still respect people’s privacy. Nobody should have to share a personal story to justify needing rest or support.

The day-to-day expectations matter just as much as the wellbeing email.

A customer service experience I still remember started with an order that went wrong.

The person who helped me didn’t make me repeat the story or transfer me around. They explained what they could do, gave me a realistic timeline, and followed up when they said they would.

Nothing dramatic. Just someone taking responsibility and keeping a promise.

By the end, I trusted the business more than I had before the problem.

It made me think about how much effort companies put into winning a customer, and how little attention sometimes goes into what happens when that customer needs help.

The follow-through is part of the product too.

MBA at INSEAD: done!

I’m happy, tired, and still getting used to the idea that it’s finished.

Thank you to the classmates who made the experience so much richer than the coursework alone. I learned a lot from the conversations between classes, the different perspectives, and the friendships that came out of it all.

To the faculty and staff, thank you for your time and care.

And to my family and friends: thank you for the encouragement, patience, and support throughout. Getting here was a shared effort, even if only my name is on the degree.

Feeling very grateful for this chapter and the people I get to take with me into the next one.

My unpopular opinion about hustle culture: working hard isn’t the problem.

Sometimes you care about something enough to put in a long week. Sometimes a deadline is real, an opportunity is unusual, or you just want to see how far you can take an idea.

The problem is turning that into a permanent expectation—and treating anyone who wants a different life as less ambitious.

There’s a big difference between choosing an intense season and being told every season has to be intense.

I respect people who work hard. I also respect people who close their laptop at five because they’ve decided what enough looks like.

You should get a say in what your ambition costs you.

My newsletter just reached 10,000 subscribers.

I wish I could point to one clever thing that made it happen. Mostly, it was sending the next issue, paying attention to replies, and slowly getting better at writing something worth opening.

A few things helped:

• Keeping a clear promise about what readers would get.
• Asking people what they found useful—and actually using their answers.
• Making it easy for someone to share an issue with a friend.
• Cutting the sections I liked writing when readers consistently skipped them.

Some issues took off. Plenty didn’t. I learned more once I stopped treating every send as a verdict on the whole project.

To everyone who reads, replies, or forwards it: thank you. You’ve helped build this.

Networking got easier for me when I stopped treating it as a room full of people I needed to impress.

If you’re introverted, a few things might help:

• Aim for one good conversation, not twenty introductions.
• Choose smaller events or one-to-one coffees when you can.
• Prepare a question you’re actually curious about. You don’t need a polished opening line.
• Follow up with something specific you talked about. “Here’s that article” goes further than a generic connection request.
• Leave yourself time to recharge. You don’t have to attend everything.

You can build a strong network quietly. Being interested, thoughtful, and reliable gives people plenty to remember you by.

Working in sales taught me to stop interpreting every “no” as a personal judgment.

Sometimes the timing is wrong. Sometimes there’s no budget. Sometimes what you’re offering just isn’t useful to that person.

It also taught me how often I was preparing my next sentence instead of listening. A good question, followed by enough silence to let someone answer, can change a conversation completely.

And I learned that promising less and following through usually beats saying whatever gets you to the next meeting.

Those lessons have followed me well beyond sales. Listen properly. Be clear about what you can do. Don’t make someone else’s decision the measure of your worth.

Our nonprofit has reached 1,000 volunteers! 💛

That number represents people making room in their lives to help: giving an afternoon, sharing a skill, showing up again, or bringing a friend along.

To every volunteer, whether you’ve just joined us or have been here for years: thank you. Your time and care make this work possible.

Thank you, too, to the people who welcome new volunteers, answer questions, and handle the practical details that keep everything moving.

We’re proud of this milestone, and even more grateful for the community behind it. Here’s to everything we’ll do together next.

Back at work after parental leave, with a very full camera roll and a lot of mixed feelings.

I’m glad to see familiar faces and use a part of my brain that’s been on a different schedule lately. I’m also missing my child and working out a routine that still feels new.

Thank you to the colleagues who covered things while I was away, and to everyone making the return feel manageable. A thoughtful handover and a little patience go a long way.

I’m finding my feet again. Some things feel familiar; others need a fresh approach.

For anyone else returning from leave: I hope you get the time and support to settle in, too.

Small agency folks: which CRM do you actually enjoy using?

We’re looking for something that makes it easy to track leads, follow up, and see where conversations stand without spending half the week maintaining it.

Would love recommendations based on real use, especially from small teams. What do you use, what does it cost, and what’s the annoying bit you only discovered after signing up?

Bonus points for straightforward setup and pricing that stays reasonable as the team grows.

Thanks in advance!

Product managers should learn enough SQL to answer a basic question without turning it into a ticket.

How many people used this feature last week? Where do new users drop off? Is that average hiding a big difference between customer groups?

Being able to explore those questions yourself speeds up your thinking. It also helps you ask better questions when you do need an analyst.

You still need to understand what the data means. A query can run perfectly and give you a misleading answer because you counted the wrong event or missed how a table works.

Start with SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, and joins. Then ask someone who knows the data to check your work.

That’s a useful investment in better product decisions.

Deep Work by Cal Newport changed how I think about a full workday.

I used to finish a day of messages, meetings, and quick requests feeling busy but oddly unsure what I’d accomplished. The book helped me see how little uninterrupted time I was giving the work that required the most thought.

The idea I’ve kept coming back to is simple: concentration needs a place in the calendar. It rarely appears on its own.

I don’t have a perfect system. But protecting a block of time, choosing one difficult task, and closing the inbox has helped more than another productivity app ever did.

A useful read if your days feel full and your important work keeps slipping to tomorrow.

Ten years as a nurse.

I think about how much I had to learn when I started, and how much there still is to learn now.

Some days stay with you because they were joyful. Others because they were heartbreaking. Often, it’s a small moment: helping someone feel less frightened, explaining something again, making sure a family knows what happens next.

I’m grateful to the colleagues who have taught me, backed me up, and understood without needing a long explanation. This work asks a lot of people, and the people beside you matter enormously.

I’m proud to be a nurse. I also know how much good nursing depends on having the time, staffing, and support to do it well.

Thank you to everyone who has been part of these ten years.

The biggest interview mistake I see as a recruiter is answering in generalities.

“I’m a strong communicator.”
“I work well under pressure.”
“I’m a team player.”

You might be all of those things. But I can’t learn much about how you work until you give me an example.

Pick a real situation. Explain what needed to happen, what you personally did, and what changed as a result. If it didn’t go well, talk about that too.

You don’t need an impressive story for every question. A clear example from an ordinary project often tells me more than a rehearsed answer full of adjectives.

Before your next interview, choose a few specific experiences you can talk through. It’s much easier than trying to invent the perfect answer on the spot.

Cloud bill creeping up faster than you expected?

We’re hosting a free webinar next Thursday on cloud cost optimization.

We’ll cover how to spot wasted spend, decide which changes are worth making, and keep costs visible as usage grows. The aim is to give you practical steps you can take back to your team.

If you’re responsible for cloud infrastructure—or just trying to understand where the money goes—we’d love to have you join us.

Interested? Send me a message for the registration details.

I’m making a career change from teaching to UX design.

There’s a lot to learn, and being a beginner again has been humbling. But I’m also finding some familiar ground: listening carefully, breaking down complicated information, noticing when someone is confused, and changing an approach when it isn’t working.

Teaching gave me years of practice paying attention to how people understand and use information. I’m excited to bring that experience into design while building the skills this new role requires.

Thank you to the people who have shared advice, given feedback, and helped me see a path into the field.

If you’ve made a similar move, I’d love to hear what helped you in the early days.

I used to say yes too quickly at work.

Yes to the extra project. Yes to the quick favour. Yes to a deadline I already knew would be difficult.

It felt helpful in the moment. Later, I’d be stretched too thin, quietly frustrated, and doing a worse job on things I’d already committed to.

I’m getting better at pausing before I answer.

“What would we move to make room for this?”
“I can do it by Friday, but not tomorrow.”
“I don’t have the capacity to take this on.”

These conversations can still feel uncomfortable. But they’re much easier than explaining a missed deadline after pretending I could do everything.

I want my yes to be something people can rely on.

So happy to see my former colleague Priya stepping into her new role as CTO!

Working with Priya, I always appreciated how thoughtfully she approached difficult problems and how much attention she gave to the people doing the work. She made space for questions, took ideas seriously, and helped the team move forward.

It’s wonderful to see her take this next step. Her new team has a lot to look forward to.

Congratulations, Priya—very well deserved! 🎉

A year into freelancing as a designer, I’ve learned that doing the design is only part of the job.

There’s also scoping the work, asking the awkward budget question, writing a clear proposal, chasing an invoice, and figuring out what to do when three projects all need attention at once.

A few lessons I’m taking into year two:

• Put the scope in writing, even when the project seems simple.
• Ask more questions before opening a design tool.
• Make room in the schedule for admin and finding the next project.
• Give clients clear updates before they have to ask.
• Price with enough breathing room to do the work properly.

I’ve loved the independence. I’ve also had weeks when I missed a predictable salary more than I expected.

Still learning, still glad I tried it. Thank you to the clients and fellow freelancers who’ve helped me through the first year.
